content: The meta-analysis lacked sufficient statistical power to detect a difference in mortality or to establish equivalence. The risk of bias in the single trial was low, and the trial was generally well-conducted. However, there was serious imprecision, as the trial lacked the power to detect or exclude clinically significant differences. Neurological sequelae in adults were rare. Inconsistencies were noted across trials. One trial reported a shorter median coma resolution time with quinine, another found no difference, and a third trial provided incomplete data on mean coma recovery time. The data could not be pooled due to serious imprecision. Despite this, the trials were generally well-conducted with a low risk of bias. Two of the largest studies demonstrated shorter median clearance times with artemether, while all four trials compared intramuscular artemether with intravenous quinine in adults across Thailand, Papua New Guinea, and Vietnam. Serious imprecision was noted as the data could not be pooled. Fever clearance times varied, with one trial favoring quinine and two favoring artemether. The trials were well-conducted with no serious risk of bias, and the findings were consistent. In Asia, older children and adults randomized to rectal artesunate had significantly higher mortality compared to placebo, though the cause remains unclear. This trial was conducted in community settings in Bangladesh, Ghana, and Tanzania. Serious imprecision was noted due to the low number of events. Allocation was concealed, and participants and staff were blinded to treatment allocation. Mass testing and treatment (MTaT) interventions were evaluated in seven studies, including four cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) in Kenya, Indonesia, Zambia, and Burkina Faso, and three non-randomized studies (NRSs) in Senegal, Ghana, and India. The cRCTs conducted 2–3 rounds of MTaT over one year, except for the Kenya study, which conducted six rounds over two years. Studies in Kenya and Burkina Faso were in moderate-to-high transmission areas, while those in Indonesia and Zambia were in low transmission areas. The overall risk of bias for community-level outcomes was low. Meta-analyses of MTaT results showed little to no reduction in community-level incidence or prevalence of infection, though two studies reported a small reduction in clinical malaria incidence. The certainty of evidence from NRSs was graded as very low. High MTaT did not reduce malaria prevalence at two months or incidence between 0–12 months. However, it likely reduced the prevalence of infection at six months but not at nine months. Evidence on adverse events was very uncertain due to serious imprecision and indirectness. Targeted drug administration (TDA) was evaluated in two studies conducted in post-elimination settings. Migrant workers were treated with full therapeutic doses of chloroquine and 14 days of primaquine. No additional infections were identified in the community for five months (Sri Lanka) or two years (Greece) after the last round of TDA. Adverse events were monitored, with one serious case of hemolysis due to an incorrect G6PD test result, while other side effects were minor. The evidence on TDA's effect on malaria prevalence was uncertain, with little to no difference observed. Serious adverse events were rare, but the evidence was limited by very serious imprecision. Non-randomized studies had a very serious risk of bias, as outcomes were collected only in the intervention arm, and effect measures could not be calculated due to the absence of control measures.
